summary: The wild river country of western Tasmania, in the heart of the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area. The tannin-dark Franklin and Gordon rivers cut gorges through rainforest and buttongrass beneath peaks such as the white quartzite dome of Frenchmans Cap. The Lyell Highway crosses the park with short walks to the Franklin and Nelson Falls; the rest is for multi-day walkers, rafters and cruise passengers from Strahan.

facts.suggestedTime: Half a day to five days

story: Water is everywhere here. With more than 1,900 millimetres of rain a year, the park lies in the wettest part of Tasmania, and the water trickles off the peaks into creeks that twist through the rocks and gather into the Franklin and Gordon rivers. The rivers are stained the colour of tea by tannins from the surrounding plants. Glaciers shaped the mountains, and from King William Saddle on the Lyell Highway you can see Frenchmans Cap, a 1,446-metre mountain of white quartzite, rising above ranges clad in rainforest.

The park holds numerous Aboriginal sites, among them caves that confirm the southernmost extent of human occupation during the last ice age, and the area remains of great spiritual significance to today's Aboriginal community. Some sites, including Kutikina Cave, have been returned to the Aboriginal community under the Aboriginal Lands Act 1995. Across the Tasmanian Wilderness, burning by Aboriginal people over tens of thousands of years helped create the buttongrass moorlands seen today.

Colonial history here began with the penal settlement on Sarah Island in Macquarie Harbour in 1822. Escaped convicts were among the first Europeans to cross these ranges, and many died in the attempt. Convicts were also the first to fell Huon pine along the lower Gordon, starting a piners' trade that lasted more than 150 years; gangs of four to six men lived for months in huts called 'badger boxes'. The Linda Track, cut in 1887 to reach the western mineral fields, was the forerunner of the Lyell Highway, which opened in 1932.

In the late 1970s and early 1980s a proposed hydro-electric dam on the Gordon below the Franklin set off the largest conservation battle ever fought in Australia, the Franklin Dam blockade. On 1 July 1983 the High Court backed the federal government's bid to preserve the wild rivers, and the Franklin still runs free. The rainforest, buttongrass and eucalypt forest shelter the Tasmanian devil and spotted-tailed and eastern quolls, and platypus feed in the river shallows.
howItWorks: The park is managed by the Tasmania Parks and Wildlife Service (PWS), and a valid parks pass is needed for entry, including at the roadside walks on the Lyell Highway; children under five are free. A Daily Pass covers one vehicle of up to eight people for 24 hours; a Holiday Pass covers all Tasmanian national parks for up to two months and suits a touring trip. Passes are sold online and at PWS visitor centres; the nearest is at Lake St Clair, east of the park. PWS reviews its fees each year in line with CPI.

Walkers heading for Frenchmans Cap must register with PWS before they go, sign the log books, and stay no more than one night at each hut; carry a tent, since hut space is not guaranteed. The whole Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area is a Fuel Stove Only Area, so campfires are prohibited all year. Follow the seven Leave No Trace principles: camp on durable surfaces, carry out all rubbish, bury toilet waste 15–20 centimetres deep at least 100 metres from water, camps and tracks, and keep wildlife wild.

The Franklin is one of the most remote and committing rivers in Tasmania, with rapids of grade 2 to 5 and some grade 6 at high water. PWS advises that only experienced paddlers, or those with a qualified guide, attempt it; most trips take about two weeks. From August to November PWS carries out planned burns in the Battlement Hills, Pleiades and Orange River areas that can close tracks, so check the alerts page before you go. Dogs and recreational drones are not allowed.

sights.name: Franklin River Nature Trail
sights.note: A 1-kilometre, 25-minute loop beside the Lyell Highway through mossy rainforest to the banks of the Franklin, the river saved from a dam. Wheelchair-friendly; walk it anticlockwise.

sights.name: Donaghys Hill
sights.note: A gentle 2.2-kilometre, 40-minute return climb to a lookout on a rocky pinnacle above the Franklin River valley, with views to Frenchmans Cap.

sights.name: Nelson Falls
sights.note: A 20-minute return boardwalk through sassafras, myrtle and ferns to a waterfall, roaring after rain, at the park's western edge on the Lyell Highway.

sights.name: Frenchmans Cap
sights.note: A 1,446-metre white quartzite peak, the goal of a 54-kilometre, three- to five-day return walk. The final scramble is unsafe in poor weather. Registration required.

sights.name: Lake Vera
sights.note: First night's stop on the Frenchmans Cap track, 15 kilometres in after a swing bridge over the Franklin; Vera Hut sleeps 20, with tent platforms nearby.

sights.name: Lake Tahune
sights.note: A lake beneath the cliffs of Frenchmans Cap, reached over exposed Barron Pass. Tahune Hut is the base for the 3.2-kilometre return climb to the summit.

sights.name: Lake Rhona
sights.note: An alpine lake hidden among the peaks of the Denison Range, reached on a 28-kilometre, two- to three-day return walk. Grade 4.

weather: This park receives more than 1,900 millimetres of rain a year, the wettest part of the state. Expect rain in any season and rivers that rise fast: the Franklin's levels can change quickly at any time of year. Snow, rain, wind and sun are all possible in any month on the high ground, and snow occasionally closes the Lyell Highway in winter. On the Frenchmans Cap track, Barron Pass and the plateau beyond are exposed to frequent strong and gusting winds, and poor visibility, ice and snow make the quartzite slippery. Rafting parties set off in summer, and walkers in any season must be ready for cold, wet and windy conditions.
directions: The Lyell Highway (A10), between Hobart and Queenstown, runs through the heart of the park. From Hobart it is about two and a half hours west to King William Saddle, the eastern boundary beyond Derwent Bridge, and about three hours to Nelson Falls, the western boundary 56 kilometres further on. From Launceston, drive south via Longford and Poatina on the Highland Lakes Road (A5) to Miena, then the B11 to Bronte Park, and join the highway. The lower Gordon River is reached by daily cruise boats from Strahan, about an hour away. Avoid driving at night, when wildlife is on the roads.

fees.title: Daily Pass, per vehicle
fees.detail: Up to 24 hours, for a vehicle of up to eight people; $24.55 per person by bus, bicycle or on foot. Not valid at Cradle Mountain. As listed by PWS in November 2026; reviewed each year by CPI.

fees.title: Holiday Pass, all Tasmanian national parks
fees.detail: Per vehicle of up to eight people for up to two months, or $49.20 per person travelling by bus, bicycle or on foot. Children under five are free.

fees.title: Annual Parks Pass
fees.detail: All Tasmanian national parks for a year, for up to two vehicles registered at the holder's address; $83.85 with an eligible concession card.

chronology.text: Aboriginal people are living in this area; their cave sites mark the southernmost human occupation of the last ice age.
A penal settlement is established on Sarah Island in Macquarie Harbour; convict piners begin felling Huon pine on the lower Gordon.
The Linda Track is cut to the western mineral fields, the forerunner of the Lyell Highway.
The Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area is declared; the park now lies at its heart.
On 1 July the High Court backs the federal government's bid to stop the Franklin Dam and preserve the wild rivers.
The Aboriginal Lands Act 1995 provides for the return of culturally significant sites, among them Kutikina Cave, to the Aboriginal community.

safety: White-water paddling on Tasmanian rivers can be highly hazardous. The Franklin has log jams and strainers requiring portages, and its water level can rise quickly; go only with experience or a qualified guide.
Frenchmans Cap is a challenging Grade 4 walk for experienced walkers, with steep climbs, ladders and exposed rocky plateau. Do not attempt the summit in wind, rain, ice, snow or poor visibility.

Deaths have occurred when walkers were caught unprepared in cold, wet and windy weather. Carry waterproof jacket and overtrousers, warm layers, a hat and gloves, and a 3–4 season tent on overnight walks.
Record your trip in the log books, tell someone your plans and carry a personal locator beacon in remote country; mobile coverage cannot be relied on.
Treat water from rainwater tanks and streams before drinking.
regulations: Fuel Stove Only Area: fires are prohibited all year.
Register before walking to Frenchmans Cap, and stay no more than one night at each hut.
Do not feed wildlife; store all food sealed inside your pack and tent, as possums rip tents to reach it.
Dogs and recreational drones are not allowed in Tasmanian national parks.
Clean boots, gear and vehicles before entering the World Heritage Area to stop the spread of plant disease.
